item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
+1 for a original idea written in a compelling way. Just had a slight suggestion, but as it's bigger than just a spelling or grammar error I didn't want to change it.

SCP-792-1 specimens will emerge headfirst in a prone position.

The wording establishes that the bodies are laying face down when they emerge. Based on the picture, my suggestion would be to change it to

SCP-792-1 specimens will emerge headfirst in a prone or supine position.

Funny enough, my only other issue with this article is also in this line. When saying "headfirst in a prone position", is that just because the back of the head would be the tallest thing on a body laying prone? What if someone with a particularly large posterior emerged?

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Copy and pasting from The Leak thread.

SCP-792 is a halfway point to the afterlife of a religion that basically decided to cut out the middleman in the conversion process and just force people to believe in it. If you happen to read any material pertaining to that religon's beliefs, be it a pamphlet, book, short paragraph, etc or hear a sermon on them, you're going to go to the 792 afterlife, no matter what religion you actually follow. Wandering around somewhere is a "prophet" that the 792 religion has drafted similarly, and are basically blackmailing into preaching for them. Instances of SCP-792-1 are still conscious, though show no signs of life.

Isaad is heaven. The ones who are worthy (note that Isaad's definition of worthy may vary greatly from traditional thought) are taken there, the ones who aren't have their souls destroyed.

item.content:encoded:
Well, not entirely meaningless, in universe. But certainly not very interesting, story-wise.

Saying that the roots have the same chemical make-up as human tissue does at least establish that they aren't made of metal, stone, inert ectoplasm, or molybdenum poly-bromide. Given what the Foundation has encountered in the past, it's not utterly useless to rule out extreme possibilities. It's just not a riveting detail for the reader.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I like this. Early on, I started thinking this was some sort of catastrophe being played out in reverse — the bodies emerging from the ground being the reverse of the bodies decaying and being absorbed into the soil.

I do find the part where the researcher suspends testing to be a bit lacking in motivation, given how the Foundation operates. What we've got is a suggestion that there will be some sort of spiritual harm to the corpses if they're not processed without interference. We'd need some indication that the researcher cared about this, or had reason to fear repercussions.

By the way, wouldn't the researchers have taken a close look at the pond?

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Not really. That describes most life on earth. Just say something like "resembling human connective tissue" or something like that.

I don't mind the discontinuation of tests. The Foundation likes to poke things, but that's secondary to ensuring they don't end up harming anyone. It's perhaps a touch hasty on no little than fairly unsubstantiated threats, but the Foundation doesn't want this blowing up in people's faces. It's Secure Contain Protect, not Test Test Test.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Agreed on both counts.

I also feel like the containment procedures - specifically the guards - are a bit much. One guard every 250m means that at the bare minimum - assuming the area is perfectly circular - you'd need 173 guards*. If it's a 10k*15k rectangle, that jumps to 200. Triple it to account for 8hr shifts, and then throw in another ~10% for sick/vacation leave. Now you've got 660 guards for a Mostly Harmless tract of empty land.

*assuming I didn't cock up my math.

Unanimously… eh, I wasn't there.

Now… I'm not sure it'd work better. The question is, what the hell are you trying to say. Is it organic material? Then that can be said more simply, and your proposed fix doesn't say any more than that. Hell, it'd be true for actual plant material.
Is it resembling particular human tissues? Tell it that way, and elaborate. Muscle tissue? Bone? Organ tissue? A layered structure containing all of those? Stem cells or something?

Also, you could keep it I like the characterisation - perhaps with the researcher getting a reprimand and the tests starting again.

That's not explained well in the article, or at all, really. There are corpses just left to moulder for almost a year. My brain just assumes this is vaguely tropical, so they're basically sludge at that point. And before the Foundation showed up and built a fence, weren't there all variety of foraging animals running around? Wouldn't this be wolf city, basically? Why aren't generic evil hazmat guys thanking us for not letting their precious crop get ate. And why did they stop testing after that one guy made a vague threat? We're the Foundation, damnit. SCP-682 can be chanting prophecies of destruction in Ancient Egyptian and we'll still by trying to find new ways to piss him off for science.

As for the article: the picture is bad, and it's colouring my entire perception. I can't tell if I don't like this because that picture just screams 'bad article', or it's actually bad.
